stances.claim: Filing a criminal case is only a beginning; vigilant follow-up by victims, private prosecutors, civil society, and the bar is what actually delivers justice.
stances.rhetorical_move: civic-pedagogy: reframes prosecution as a sustained citizen practice rather than a State function
stances.evidence: Ragos case as live example; SC resolutions documenting 40% dismissal-by-attrition and 80% criminal-share of backlog

stances.claim: Defective informations — those failing to allege essential elements — are a major engine of acquittal and case dismissal, as shown in the GMA plunder dismissal and the Mamasapano graft acquittal.
stances.rhetorical_move: exemplar-cascade: stacks three high-profile failures to evidence a systemic drafting problem
stances.evidence: GMA dismissal for missing 'main plunderer' allegation; Purisima/Napeñas acquittal for missing 'material remuneration' allegation; Marcos cases dismissed for failure to authenticate documents

stances.claim: The structural failures of docket management — prosecutor and witness no-shows, PAO lawyer shortages, complainant attrition — guarantee that filing alone cannot deliver justice without vigilance and reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: data-driven structural diagnosis using the SC's own admissions
stances.evidence: SC resolutions of March 18 2014, Jan 8 2013, Sept 4 2012

stances.claim: Even after final-judgment victories, adjudged civil liability often remains uncollected, requiring sustained help from the IBP and legal academe.
stances.rhetorical_move: uncomfortable-closure: highlights the gap between formal victory and actual recovery
stances.evidence: Author's own 4/12/20 column calling for IBP help, still unanswered

notable_anecdotes: The grade-school adage 'Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty' deployed as the column's organizing aphorism, extended to 'It is also the price of speedy justice.'

GMA's plunder acquittal after the prosecution had already rested and before she could even begin her defense — used as the column's most dramatic example of how a faulty information can destroy a case after years of trial.
Mamasapano massacre acquittals of Purisima and Napeñas because the information 'failed to allege a crime' — failing to state material remuneration as an element.
Author's prior call to the IBP (4/12/20 column) for help closing graft cases — silently unanswered.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban uses the Quezon City Police's homicide filing against MSgt. Daniel Florendo Jr. for the fatal shooting of retired Army Cpl. Winston Ragos to argue that filing a criminal case is only the beginning -- sustained vigilance is the real price of speedy justice. He explains the limits of private-prosecutor participation (subordinate to public prosecutors, scoped to civil damages) and walks through three exemplary failures: GMA's plunder acquittal because the information failed to allege the 'identity of the main plunderer' (an essential element) after the prosecution had already rested; the Mamasapano acquittals of Purisima and Napeñas because the Anti-Graft information omitted material remuneration as an element; and the Marcos ill-gotten wealth dismissals for failure to authenticate documentary evidence. He then catalogues the structural causes of clogged dockets using the Supreme Court's own resolutions -- the March 18, 2014 trial-duration mandate frustrated by Rules-of-Court exceptions, the January 8, 2013 admission that 80 percent of trial-court backlog is criminal and stems from prosecutor and witness absences and PAO lawyer shortages, and the September 4, 2012 admission that roughly 40 percent of criminal cases are dismissed annually because complainants 'simply gave up' after repeated postponements. He closes with the uncomfortable observation that even final-judgment victories often leave civil liability uncollected, renewing his earlier call to the IBP for help -- a call that, he candidly notes, has gone unanswered.
